subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic selection when cannabis co-morbidity is dominant
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the early psychosis service reviewing a 20 year old university student with 3 weeks of increasingly disorganised speech, persecutory delusions that his housemates are recording him, and third-person auditory hallucinations. He has been smoking around 3 g of high-potency cannabis daily for 18 months, with insight lost 4 weeks ago. He is otherwise physically well. There is a paternal uncle with schizophrenia. He has no prior psychiatric contact. He is currently residing with his mother who has agreed to support him at home during any pharmacotherapy trial.

He accepts oral treatment and refuses depot injection at this stage.

data_table.MSE: disorganised speech, persecutory delusions, third-person AH, no suicidal ideation, insight impaired
data_table.Bloods: urea, electrolytes, LFTs, TSH, glucose, lipids, prolactin within normal limits
data_table.Urine drug screen: positive THC, negative amphetamines, cocaine, opioids
data_table.Weight: 78 kg, BMI 24, fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HDL 1.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oral antipsychotic choice?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg nocte titrated to 20 mg as first-line therapy given its rapid effect and reliable response
options.rationale: Olanzapine has substantial metabolic burden (weight gain 5-12 kg in first year) and is not recommended first-line in first episode psychosis per RANZCP; risperidone or aripiprazole are preferred for their metabolic profile and dopaminergic effect. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Chlorpromazine 100 mg three times daily as a broad spectrum first line agent with mild sedative benefit for sleep
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics carry high EPS risk and are not first-line in first episode psychosis; second-generation agents (risperidone or aripiprazole) are standard. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Clozapine 12.5 mg twice daily titrated to 300 mg to address treatment-resistant cannabis-related psychosis quickly
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of 2 antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration); it is not first-line in first episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Risperidone 1 mg twice daily titrated to 2 to 4 mg over 1 week with monitoring for extrapyramidal side effects
options.rationale: Risperidone or aripiprazole are first-line in first episode psychosis per RANZCP CPG because of the more favourable metabolic profile; low starting dose with weekly titration to 2-4 mg is standard, with EPS monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

options.text: Quetiapine 300 mg nocte titrated to 600 mg as first line agent to improve sleep and reduce paranoid ideation
options.rationale: Quetiapine is used but has weaker antipsychotic effect at low doses and is often subtherapeutic; risperidone or aripiprazole are preferred first-line per RANZCP with better response in first episode psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

explanation.summary: First episode psychosis carries a favourable response rate to low-dose second-generation antipsychotics; RANZCP recommends risperidone or aripiprazole first-line because of the metabolic profile relative to olanzapine and clozapine. Start low and titrate slowly (risperidone 1 mg BD to 2-4 mg total; aripiprazole 10 mg to 15 mg daily) with monitoring for EPS. Substance use co-management (cannabis in particular) is essential as continued use predicts poorer response and relapse. Family psychoeducation and vocational support are cornerstones. Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring (weight, waist, glucose, lipids, BP) is required.
key_points: Risperidone or aripiprazole first-line in first episode
Low starting dose, slow titration, EPS monitoring
Cannabis co-management essential
Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring
explanation.pearls: Around 60-80 percent of first episode psychosis responds within 6 weeks to adequate dose; treatment for at least 12 to 24 months after remission is standard, with individualised discussion around continuation, given up to 80 percent relapse rate if stopped after single episode remission.

subtopic_detail: SSRI selection when breastfeeding an exclusively breastfed newborn
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatrist reviewing a 32 year old G1P1 who is 6 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding a term male infant. She reports 4 weeks of pervasive low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia, guilt about not enjoying her baby, and early morning waking. EPDS score today is 18. She has passive suicidal ideation without plan and no thoughts of harming her baby. She has good social support with her partner and her mother visiting daily. Sleep is fragmented but the baby is feeding and gaining weight well. She has no personal history of depression prior to this pregnancy.

She would prefer to continue breastfeeding if safe to do so and asks about medication options today.

data_table.MSE: flat affect, tearful, thought content of guilt and hopelessness, no psychosis, passive SI no plan, insight intact
data_table.Infant: 6 week old term male, exclusively breastfed, gaining weight along 50th centile
data_table.Bloods: TSH, iron studies, ferritin, B12 within normal limits, no anaemia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line SSRI to prescribe?

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg daily as the first line SSRI in breastfeeding with review at 2 weeks for response and tolerability
options.rationale: Sertraline has the strongest safety data in breastfeeding, with negligible infant serum levels and low relative infant dose (<2 percent); it is first-line SSRI in perinatal depression per Beyond Blue and LactMed. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily as first line agent, with reduction to alternate day dosing if the infant develops symptoms
options.rationale: Fluoxetine and its active metabolite norfluoxetine have long half-lives (2-4 days and 7-15 days respectively), leading to higher infant serum levels compared to sertraline; sertraline or paroxetine are preferred in breastfeeding. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

options.text: Escitalopram 10 mg daily as it has a favourable side effect profile and gentle onset for postnatal use in mothers
options.rationale: Escitalopram is second-line in breastfeeding; sertraline has more robust safety data and lower relative infant dose in the perinatal literature. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

options.text: Venlafaxine XR 75 mg daily as an SNRI to address concurrent anxiety symptoms with the depressed mood presenting
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has less breastfeeding safety data than sertraline and is not first-line perinatally; SSRIs (sertraline preferred) are first-line for depression with mixed anxiety features in breastfeeding mothers. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

options.text: St John's wort standardised extract 300 mg three times daily as a natural alternative for mild to moderate depression
options.rationale: St John's wort is not recommended in breastfeeding due to inconsistent standardisation, drug interactions (CYP3A4 inducer), and infant safety uncertainty; sertraline is first-line. (Source: LactMed Sertraline)

explanation.summary: Postnatal depression affects around 10-15 percent of new mothers and warrants active treatment given impact on infant attachment, cognitive and emotional development. Sertraline has the strongest breastfeeding safety data of the SSRIs, with negligible infant serum levels and no reported adverse effects at therapeutic maternal doses. Start 50 mg daily (25 mg for the first 3 days if anxious features) and review at 2 weeks. Psychological therapy (interpersonal therapy or CBT) is offered concurrently. Postpartum psychosis or severe depression with active suicidal or infanticidal ideation warrants urgent psychiatric admission with mother-baby unit consideration.
key_points: Sertraline first-line SSRI in breastfeeding (low RID)
Paroxetine also acceptable in breastfeeding
Fluoxetine higher infant serum levels (long half-life)
IPT or CBT concurrent psychological therapy
explanation.pearls: The relative infant dose (RID) for sertraline is around 0.5-2 percent of maternal weight-adjusted dose; the general threshold of concern is 10 percent; monitor infant for sedation, feeding, weight gain, and irritability.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic clarification when cognitive complaints coexist
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 74 year old retired teacher accompanied by his wife with 6 months of progressive loss of interest, low energy, appetite loss with 5 kg weight loss, and complaints of poor memory and concentration. His wife reports he says he is a burden. He denies suicidal plans. On testing he scores poorly on serial 7s citing lack of effort, but recall is intact with cueing. His Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination is 82 out of 100 with a global reduction (not domain-specific). CT brain 6 months ago was unremarkable for atrophy or vascular changes.

He has hypertension controlled with perindopril and no other medications.

data_table.MSE: flat affect, psychomotor slowing, thought content of guilt and worthlessness, no psychosis, passive suicidal ideation no plan
data_table.Cognitive: ACE 82/100 with global reduction, recall improves with semantic cueing, no focal deficits
data_table.Bloods: TSH, B12, folate, calcium, urea, electrolytes, LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Refer for donepezil trial as a therapeutic diagnostic step for early Alzheimer's disease with treatment response
options.rationale: Cognitive picture with intact recall on cueing, global (not domain-specific) reduction, and depressive symptoms fits pseudodementia rather than Alzheimer's; treating depression first clarifies the diagnosis and avoids inappropriate cholinesterase inhibitor exposure. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Refer for immediate lumbar puncture and CSF amyloid biomarkers before any medication trial to establish diagnosis clearly
options.rationale: CSF biomarkers are not first-line in this scenario where depression is a strong alternative explanation; treat depression first, then reassess cognition and consider structural imaging or biomarker referral if deficits persist. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg daily titrated to 50 mg with cognitive reassessment at 8 to 12 weeks after remission achieved
options.rationale: Depressive pseudodementia is common in late-life depression; recall improving with cueing, global cognitive reduction, and prominent depressive features support depression as primary; treat with an SSRI at reduced starting dose (elderly), then reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Order MRI brain with hippocampal volumes prior to any treatment intervention to define underlying neurodegeneration presence
options.rationale: MRI is useful when structural cause is suspected but should not delay treatment of clearly identified depression; treat first and image if cognitive deficits persist after mood remission. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

options.text: Start memantine 5 mg daily titrated to 20 mg for suspected moderate Alzheimer's disease as a therapeutic diagnostic step
options.rationale: Memantine is for moderate to severe Alzheimer's, not a diagnostic trial; and the clinical picture supports pseudodementia rather than established dementia at this point. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Depressive pseudodementia is late-life depression presenting with prominent cognitive complaints. Distinguishing features from Alzheimer's disease include prominent affective symptoms, insight into cognitive change (complaining rather than concealing), global rather than domain-specific cognitive reduction, recall improving with cueing, poor effort on testing, and preserved autobiographical memory. Treat depression with an SSRI at reduced starting dose (elderly) and reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission. Persistent cognitive deficits after mood remission warrant further neurodegenerative workup including MRI and neuropsychology.
key_points: Pseudodementia: prominent depression, insight preserved
Recall improves with cueing (not seen in Alzheimer's)
SSRI first-line, reduced starting dose in elderly
Reassess cognition 8-12 weeks after mood remission
explanation.pearls: Up to 40 percent of pseudodementia patients develop true dementia within 5 years; ongoing cognitive monitoring is warranted even after mood remission; consider MRI, neuropsychology, and possible CSF biomarkers if cognition does not fully recover.

subtopic_detail: Escalation pathway when non-pharmacological measures have failed
stem:
You are the child and adolescent psychiatry registrar reviewing a 15 year old boy with autism spectrum disorder (level 3, minimally verbal) and moderate intellectual disability. His mother reports 3 months of escalating head-banging producing scalp abrasions, biting his hand producing skin breaks, and hitting his siblings when transitions occur. A structured behavioural plan with visual schedules, sensory environment modification, and functional communication training has been implemented by his ABA team for 3 months with limited response. Sleep is 4 hours per night. Medical review has excluded pain (dental, constipation, otitis).

He has never been on psychotropic medication.

data_table.Diagnostic: ASD level 3, minimally verbal, moderate ID (WISC-V IQ 45)
data_table.Behaviour: SIB (head banging, self biting) plus aggression at transitions
data_table.Medical workup: no dental caries, no otitis media, no constipation, urinalysis clear
data_table.Non-pharmacological: 3 months structured ABA and visual schedule with limited response

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Melatonin 3 mg nocte only, targeting sleep with the hope this reduces daytime irritability and self injurious behaviour
options.rationale: Melatonin may help sleep initiation but does not treat established self-injurious behaviour or aggression; when behavioural measures have failed and injury risk is present, targeted pharmacotherapy is indicated. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

options.text: Clonidine 25 micrograms nocte for arousal reduction and hyperactivity as an alternative to antipsychotic exposure
options.rationale: Clonidine is used for ADHD-symptom overlap and sleep in autism but has weaker evidence than risperidone or aripiprazole for irritability and self injurious behaviour of the severity described. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg twice daily as first line to reduce agitation and self injurious behaviour at difficult transition periods
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines cause paradoxical disinhibition in autism and intellectual disability and are not first-line; risperidone or aripiprazole is preferred with better evidence. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

options.text: Fluoxetine 10 mg daily as first line for rigid repetitive behaviours with plan to add antipsychotic only if it fails
options.rationale: SSRIs have limited evidence for irritability and aggression in autism and may worsen agitation, particularly in intellectual disability; risperidone or aripiprazole is preferred for irritability with SIB. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

options.text: Risperidone 0.25 mg nocte, titrating slowly to 0.5 mg BD, with metabolic monitoring baseline and every 3 months planned
options.rationale: Risperidone (or aripiprazole) is TGA-indicated for irritability and aggression in autism when behavioural interventions have failed; slow titration and metabolic baseline plus 3-monthly monitoring are required to minimise weight gain, hyperprolactinaemia, and metabolic burden. (Source: RCH Melbourne Autism Behaviour Guideline)

explanation.summary: Escalating self-injurious behaviour and aggression in an autistic adolescent with intellectual disability warrants a structured medical (rule out pain, constipation, dental, otitis) and behavioural (functional analysis, visual schedules, sensory adaptations) assessment first. When these are optimised and injury risk remains, risperidone or aripiprazole are the two agents with the strongest evidence and TGA indication in Australia for irritability associated with autism. Titrate slowly from a low starting dose (risperidone 0.25 mg nocte) with metabolic baseline (weight, waist, glucose, lipids, prolactin, BP) and monitoring every 3 months. Reassess indication regularly and taper when clinically stable.
key_points: Rule out pain, constipation, dental, otitis before pharmacotherapy
Risperidone or aripiprazole first-line for autism irritability
Metabolic baseline and 3-monthly monitoring
Reassess indication and taper when stable
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole tends to cause less weight gain and hyperprolactinaemia than risperidone but higher akathisia; both have TGA approval for autism-associated irritability; typical response emerges within 2-4 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Wells score with age-adjusted D-dimer threshold
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman with 24 hours of pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea. She had a total knee replacement 3 weeks ago and is mobilising with a frame at home. She has no haemoptysis, no leg swelling, and no history of malignancy. On examination she is haemodynamically stable with clear chest and no calf swelling or tenderness. Her chest X-ray is unremarkable. Her Wells score is 4.5 (surgery in last 4 weeks 1.5, PE as likely as alternative 3). An age-adjusted D-dimer using the 500 x age formula returns a value of 700 micrograms/L (age-adjusted cut-off 780).

Her creatinine is 92 micromol/L and eGFR is 62.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform CT pulmonary angiography as the Wells score of 4.5 places her in the PE-likely group requiring imaging
options.rationale: Two-level Wells >4 places the patient in the PE-likely group where CTPA is indicated regardless of D-dimer; her Wells of 4.5 with normal renal function makes CTPA the imaging of choice. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

options.text: Discharge with reassurance because the age-adjusted D-dimer is below the cut-off for her age at 780 today value
options.rationale: D-dimer strategies (standard or age-adjusted) are only validated in PE-unlikely groups (Wells <=4); a moderate to high probability Wells score requires imaging regardless of D-dimer. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

options.text: CT pulmonary angiogram given the moderate Wells probability, notwithstanding the negative age-adjusted D-dimer today
options.rationale: With a Wells score of 4.5 (PE likely, >4) the age-adjusted D-dimer strategy is NOT applicable; D-dimer testing is reserved for Wells <=4 (PE unlikely); imaging is required regardless of D-dimer in Wells >4. However Wells 4.5 puts patient in the PE-likely group so CTPA is warranted. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

options.text: Ventilation-perfusion scan first-line as the initial imaging modality due to her age and preserved renal function level
options.rationale: V/Q scan is an alternative when CTPA is contraindicated (contrast allergy, severe renal impairment, pregnancy); with eGFR 62 CTPA is safer and faster for interpretation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

options.text: Bilateral lower limb Doppler ultrasound as a proxy investigation to avoid contrast exposure with age-related nephropathy risk
options.rationale: Doppler ultrasound of legs is used to detect DVT when PE is suspected and imaging is not immediately available; a positive DVT plus clinical PE suspicion treats as PE, but with eGFR 62 CTPA is not contraindicated and is the definitive investigation. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society ANZ 2021)

explanation.summary: PE diagnostic strategy uses Wells score to stratify patients into PE-unlikely (Wells <=4) or PE-likely (Wells >4). In PE-unlikely, D-dimer (age-adjusted for over 50 using age x 10 in micrograms/L) rules out PE when below cut-off. In PE-likely, D-dimer is bypassed and imaging is performed regardless. CT pulmonary angiography is first-line unless contrast contraindicated (severe renal impairment eGFR <30, contrast allergy, pregnancy) when V/Q scan is preferred. Doppler of legs supports diagnosis if positive but does not exclude PE if negative.
key_points: Wells >4 = PE-likely: image regardless of D-dimer
Wells <=4 plus age-adjusted D-dimer below cut-off rules out PE
CTPA first-line if renal function adequate
V/Q scan when CTPA contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Age-adjusted D-dimer cut-off (age x 10 mcg/L) reduces false positives in >50s from around 40 to 25 percent without affecting negative predictive value; adopted in AU and European guidelines but the standard 500 mcg/L cut-off remains used in some centres.

subtopic_detail: Membrane stabilisation and shift plus removal choices
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68 year old man on haemodialysis who missed his last two sessions because he was interstate for a family bereavement. He presents with generalised weakness, palpitations, and nausea. He is on perindopril and spironolactone for cardiomyopathy. His observations show bradycardia and normotension. His ECG shows peaked T waves throughout, PR prolongation to 240 ms, and a QRS complex 130 ms without loss of P waves. Serum potassium is markedly raised. He has functioning tunnelled dialysis catheter access already in situ.

Nephrology is arranging urgent dialysis to run within the next 45 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 48, blood pressure 128/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.ECG: peaked T waves, PR 240 ms, QRS 130 ms, no loss of P waves, no arrhythmia
data_table.Bloods: potassium 7.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), sodium 138 mmol/L, urea 32 mmol/L, creatinine 720 micromol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 6.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: perindopril 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, carvedilol 6.25 mg BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Withhold treatment until formal potassium result is repeated to rule out haemolysis and dialysis is ready to commence
options.rationale: The ECG changes confirm the biochemical hyperkalaemia; awaiting repeat testing risks cardiac arrest during the wait. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g stat with repeat 8 hourly while awaiting haemodialysis for potassium removal today
options.rationale: Resonium is a slow-acting cation exchange resin with modest effect and does not address life-threatening ECG changes; membrane stabilisation with calcium is the immediate step. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg alone with cessation of perindopril and spironolactone while awaiting the dialysis session
options.rationale: Salbutamol lowers potassium modestly by around 0.5-1.0 mmol/L but does not stabilise the myocardium; calcium is the immediate priority in ECG changes of this severity. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 10 minutes as first-line treatment for the wide complex and metabolic acidosis today
options.rationale: Bicarbonate has role in severe metabolic acidosis but does not stabilise the myocardium acutely; calcium precedes bicarbonate and shift strategies in acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent solution followed by insulin-dextrose shift and immediate haemodialysis when available
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with peaked T waves, PR prolongation, and QRS widening requires immediate IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent for membrane stabilisation, then insulin-dextrose (10 units actrapid with 50 mL of 50 percent glucose) for shift, and dialysis for definitive removal in this ESRD patient. (Source: eTG Complete Acute Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (>=6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes) is a medical emergency treated in three parallel steps: membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent (or calcium chloride 5-10 mL of 10 percent via central line) repeated as needed; potassium shift with insulin-dextrose (10 units actrapid with 50 mL of 50 percent glucose) and nebulised salbutamol 10-20 mg; and definitive removal with haemodialysis in ESRD, or resonium and diuretics in preserved renal function. Cease contributing drugs (ACE inhibitor, ARB, spironolactone, NSAID). Continuous cardiac monitoring is essential.
key_points: IV calcium first for ECG changes (membrane stabilisation)
Insulin-dextrose plus salbutamol for shift
Haemodialysis for definitive removal in ESRD
Cease ACEI, ARB, spironolactone, NSAID
explanation.pearls: Calcium gluconate onset is 1-3 minutes with duration 30-60 minutes; repeat if ECG unchanged 5 minutes after first dose; calcium chloride has three times the elemental calcium of calcium gluconate but requires central access due to sclerosant risk.

sources.label: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for CKD
